To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the jet tomography of the quark gluon plasma can be used to determine the properties of the medium, including its temperature, density and the nature of the interaction between the jet and the medium.

the jet quenching in the QGP is sensitive to the medium-induced parton shower and that the jet tomography is an effective method to constrain the medium-induced shower and the quark and gluons energy loss in the QGP.

jet tomography is a powerful tool to constrain the energy-loss mechanism and that the next-to-leading order jet cross section is an important ingredient to achieve a reliable description of the jet quenching phenomenon.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physics of jets produced in high energy nucleus-nucleus reactions.

the study of the quark and gluons dynamics in a dense strongly interacting medium, the quark-gluon plasma (QGP), which is formed in high-energy nucleus collisions at the Relativistic Heavy-Ion Collider (RHIC).
the physics of the strong interactions at the highest energies available in nature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data are consistent with an in-medium parton shower with a medium-induced partonic splitting kernel of a type similar to the vacuum splitting kernel.
jet tomography is a promising tool for studying the properties of the quark gluon plasma created in heavy ion collisions.

the observed suppression of high-p(T) hadrons in Au + Au collisions at RHIC can be understood as due to jet quenching, and that the data provide evidence that the energy loss is large and occurs in a hot and dense medium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the jet tomography of high energy heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and the LHC can provide a powerful probe for the QCD parton shower dynamics in the hot and dense medium produced in these collisions.
the jet tomography is a promising tool for the study of the properties of the strongly interacting matter created in heavy ion collisions at RHIC and LHC.
we have developed the first fully differential next-to-leading-order calculation of jet observables in heavy-ion reactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
jet tomography is an extremely powerful tool to probe the dynamics of strongly interacting matter.
jet observables can be used as tomographic probes of the medium created in heavy-ion collisions.
jet tomography can be used as a powerful new tool to study the properties of QCD matter at extreme energy densities.
